questions.scenario: Riverton City's housing team runs a shared Claude Project called 'Tenancy Q&A' that about 30 officers and 200 residents use. Officers have started asking it to draft inspection visit reports and to write letters to landlords, because the instructions say 'answer tenancy questions clearly and helpfully' and nothing stops them.
questions.stem: What is the MOST useful change to how this Project is set up?

options.text: Add a line to the instructions: 'Answer tenancy questions only. Politely decline requests to draft letters or reports.'
Rewrite the instructions so they name precisely which tasks belong here — answering residents' questions about rights, timescales and process — and say what the Project is not for.
Create a second Project for drafting work and tell officers to use it, leaving the current instructions unchanged.
Restrict the Project to officers only and have residents' questions answered by a named team member instead.

questions.explanation: The Project has **no stated scope**, so 'helpfully' has licensed four different jobs. Instructions that describe what the Project is for are what stop the drift — and stating what it is not for matters as much, because residents' drafting requests are reasonable and will keep arriving. A prohibition line is a band-aid on a scope problem; a second Project leaves the first one open to the same drift.

whyWrong.A: A single refusal line suppresses the symptom while the underlying gap remains: an instruction set that does not say what the Project is for. Officers who hit the line will ask for the exception or start a new Project with the same wording.
whyWrong.C: Moving drafting elsewhere does nothing about why officers asked for it in the first place, and it leaves the original Project still described only as helping with tenancy questions.
whyWrong.D: Removing residents from the Project discards the reason it exists and creates a manual bottleneck, without addressing the unbounded scope that caused the problem.

questions.mindset: A shared Project needs instructions that say what it is for and what it is not for, or it absorbs every job its users can think of.

questions.scenario: Halcyon Legal's knowledge team built a Project for drafting witness statements. They put the firm's statement template, the current practice directions, three approved example statements and a twelve-page guide on interview technique into the Project's knowledge. Drafts are long, formal and often cite provisions of practice directions that the guide and the approved examples disagree about.
questions.stem: What is the MOST useful structural change?

options.text: Add an instruction telling Claude to prefer the practice directions over the guide and examples when they conflict.
Remove the twelve-page technique guide and the examples, so that only the current practice directions remain as knowledge.

Separate the material by what it is authoritative for: the practice directions as the source of procedural requirements, the template as the required structure, and the examples and the guide as illustrations only, with the instructions saying which role each plays.
Ask for shorter statements, since the length is what is allowing conflicting material to surface.

questions.explanation: Three sources that disagree produce exactly this symptom, and no precedence rule fixes it reliably because the conflict is between material that is authoritative for different things. The fix is to **make each source's role explicit** — procedural requirements here, structure there, illustration elsewhere — so the model is not choosing between them. Reducing length or removing material treats the disagreement as noise rather than as an unlabelled hierarchy.

whyWrong.A: A blanket precedence rule says the practice directions win, which is right about procedure and wrong about everything the guide covers. The conflict is real and topical, not a simple ordering problem.
whyWrong.B: Deleting the guide and examples removes the illustrations that make the firm's style legible, and it leaves the underlying problem — unlabelled sources — intact for whatever is added next.
whyWrong.D: Length is a symptom, not the cause. A tighter statement would still have to choose between two conflicting sources on procedure.

questions.mindset: When knowledge sources disagree, label what each is authoritative for; a blanket precedence rule only works if the conflict really is a simple ordering.

questions.scenario: An office manager at Fenmoor Group writes a short instruction into her Project every time she asks for a different kind of summary: 'keep it under 200 words', 'put the risks first', 'use last quarter's numbers', 'don't mention the supplier by name'. The Project has been in use for three weeks.
questions.stem: What is the BEST judgement about where these belong?

options.text: Only rules that apply every single time belong in the Project's instructions. These belong in the individual request, typed alongside the specific job.
They all belong in the Project instructions, because anything written down once is cheaper than typing it again.
They belong in her account-wide settings, so they apply in every chat as well as in the Project.
They should be kept in a shared document that she links to from each request, since instructions cannot be scoped this precisely.

questions.explanation: The test for Project instructions is whether the rule holds **every time**. 'Keep it under 200 words' for one brief and 'use last quarter's numbers' for a specific report are properties of those jobs, not of the Project — typed into the request they apply exactly where they should. Rules that accumulate in the instruction set on incident are the main reason a Project's behaviour becomes unpredictable within weeks.

whyWrong.B: Cheaper to type is not the criterion. Rules that only hold for some requests narrow every other answer, and by the fourth one the instruction set is longer than the work it describes.
whyWrong.C: Account-wide settings apply everywhere, including chats about unrelated matters, where 'use last quarter's numbers' and 'under 200 words' would distort the output.
whyWrong.D: A link cannot be applied to a chat, so it adds a step without producing the behaviour. The granularity she wants is already available by putting the rule in the request.

questions.mindset: A rule belongs in the Project only if it is true every time; otherwise it belongs in the individual request.

questions.scenario: Silverbrook Foods' technical services team uses a Project that answers plant engineers' questions from equipment manuals. Six engineers share it. One engineer added the current version of the plant's lockout procedure 'so it is covered'. Since then, questions about lockout return answers combining the procedure with two archived copies of it that were uploaded at different times.
questions.stem: Which TWO changes would address this? Choose TWO.

options.text: Delete the two archived copies of the lockout procedure, leaving only the current version as knowledge.
Add an instruction stating that when documents cover the same procedure, the one with the most recent approval date in its text is the one to follow.
Move the lockout procedure out of the Project and have engineers keep it to hand, so the Project holds only manuals.
Add the current procedure to every individual request as well as keeping it in knowledge, so it is always the most prominent version.

questions.explanation: Two things are wrong and both need addressing. **Superseded material should not be there at all** — keeping old versions of a procedure in a knowledge base is how safety-critical answers get blended. And until the next version lands, a rule about which document wins is a cheap safeguard for anything else that duplicates. Keeping the procedure out of the Project or re-pasting it in every request does not address why the answers became blended.

whyWrong.C: Lockout questions are exactly the kind engineers expect the Project to answer, and the procedure is legitimate reference material. Removing it makes the Project worse at its real job without removing the duplicate-copy risk.
whyWrong.D: Adding the procedure to every request lengthens every interaction and still leaves the archived copies loaded in the Project. It manages salience rather than removing the conflict.

questions.mindset: Superseded documents in a knowledge base should be deleted, and a tie-break rule should cover anything that duplicates while the next version is pending.

questions.scenario: Northgate Logistics wants six depots to ask Claude the same 30 operational questions and get the same answers. Two approaches are proposed. Approach one: a shared Project whose instructions and knowledge are maintained centrally. Approach two: a written one-page guide telling depot staff what to type, which each depot manager keeps and adapts locally.
questions.stem: What is the key difference between these two approaches?

options.text: Approach one guarantees identical answers everywhere; approach two lets answers vary between depots and can drift apart over time.
Approach one is cheaper to run, while approach two costs nothing but staff reading time.
They are equivalent in practice, because in both cases a human decides what Claude is told.
Approach two gives depots more flexibility, which is why it produces more accurate answers for local conditions.

questions.explanation: A shared Project applies its instructions and knowledge **automatically to every chat inside it**, and there is one copy to update. A guide depends on every person in every depot typing the same thing, applying it consistently, and updating their copy when the rules change — so variation is expected and drift over time is close to inevitable. For questions with a single right answer, that is the whole distinction.

whyWrong.B: This inverts the cost. A shared Project has a small central upkeep cost; a guide has a distributed one, paid in six managers' time and in the retraining needed after every rule change.
whyWrong.C: They differ in where the decision is enforced. A Project applies it on every chat; a guide asks a human to apply it every time, which is exactly the step that fails quietly.
whyWrong.D: Flexibility about local conditions is a real need, but the question is about 30 shared operational questions with one correct answer. Nothing here suggests local variation is the requirement being served.

questions.mindset: Instructions applied automatically to every chat cannot drift; instructions people are asked to remember will.

questions.scenario: A training coordinator at Ivybridge College has built a Project that turns staff-meeting notes into minutes. It works well for her because she has added a note at the top of the instructions: 'I am the estates officer — use our floor names and our contractor list.' Her colleague in admissions opened the same Project and found that Claude referred to 'the library' instead of 'the learning centre' and invented a contractor name.
questions.stem: What is the BEST explanation and fix?

options.text: Her note is one person's local detail in shared instructions, so it makes the Project less reliable for everyone else. Move the local naming into each request, or into a separate Project, and keep only what holds for all users in the shared instructions.
The Project is correct and the colleague is misusing it, so she should be asked to add her own note at the top of the instructions as well.
The contractor name was invented because the Project lacks the contractor list, so the fix is to upload it into the knowledge.
Her note is good practice and should be copied into a second, identical note written from the admissions team's point of view.

questions.explanation: Instructions written as 'I am the estates officer' describe **one user's context**, and in a shared Project they quietly become everyone's context. The invented contractor name follows directly: her note tells Claude a contractor list exists for estates, so the admissions user gets a confident name from an absent source. What belongs in shared instructions is what holds for all users; what is local goes in the request or in its own Project.

whyWrong.B: Asking each user to add their own note produces exactly the conflict already present — competing local statements about the same shared world — and leaves the Project unusable to anyone who has not read it.
whyWrong.C: Uploading a contractor list would put real data behind the expectation her note created, but it treats a symptom of a mis-scoped instruction as a missing file. The instruction's assumption is the problem.
whyWrong.D: A second note from admissions in the same instruction set makes the contradiction explicit rather than resolving it, and both will apply to every chat in the Project.

questions.mindset: In shared instructions, write rules that are true for every user — local context written once becomes everyone's context.

questions.scenario: A compliance officer at a health insurer wants to use Claude to draft replies to regulator enquiries. Each enquiry quotes paragraphs from the insurer's own internal claims manual, and her replies must be consistent with that manual.
questions.stem: Which material should she put in the Project's knowledge?

options.text: The current version of the claims manual only, plus the insurer's approved response templates.
Every version of the claims manual ever issued, so the replies can reflect how the guidance has evolved.
Nothing — she should paste the relevant paragraph of the manual into each enquiry she receives.
The current manual, the approved templates, and a note in the instructions saying never to quote a paragraph the manual does not support.

questions.explanation: She needs the **current** manual as the authority and the templates so the format is consistent, plus an instruction that makes the boundary explicit: anything not supported by the manual is not to be produced. That last element is what converts 'reply consistently with the manual' from an aspiration into something the output can be checked against — and it is what you would want when a regulator quotes the manual back at you.

whyWrong.A: The current manual and templates are the right starting material, but without a rule about unsupported content the replies can still contain claims the manual does not make — which is precisely what she will be held to.
whyWrong.B: Superseded versions in a knowledge base are how a reply ends up quoting a withdrawn paragraph. How guidance has evolved is a question about archives, not about a knowledge base that answers enquiries.
whyWrong.C: Pasting the paragraph per enquiry guarantees the rest of the manual is absent, and it makes consistency a matter of what she remembers to include.

questions.mindset: Put the current authority and the format templates in knowledge, and add an explicit rule about what must never be produced.

questions.scenario: Torrington Water's customer-service team has a Project holding the current tariff document. In April the tariff changed, the team uploaded the new document, and the finance team later archived the old one out of the shared drive — so the Project now holds a document that no longer exists anywhere else. A supervisor who remembers the April figure is disputing what customers have been told.
questions.stem: What is the MOST appropriate response?

options.text: The Project holds a document that exists nowhere else, so treat it as a historical record: label it clearly as superseded, keep the current tariff as the source to answer from, and add a short instruction saying which document takes precedence for current figures.
Delete the old tariff from the Project immediately, since superseded material is the only source of the discrepancy.
Do nothing, because a tariff that was correct when uploaded was correct and the Project's behaviour has not changed.
Ask the finance team to restore the old document to the shared drive so the two copies can be compared.

questions.explanation: Two facts collide: the April document is **no longer current** and it is now **the only surviving copy**, which matters for dispute handling. Labelling it as superseded keeps the historic figure available and auditable while an instruction about precedence tells the model which document answers a current-figs question. Deleting it destroys the record; ignoring it leaves a live risk that the Project answers from a withdrawn tariff.

whyWrong.B: Deleting removes the copy that cannot be recovered from elsewhere. It solves the blending problem by destroying the evidence, and the supervisor's dispute is precisely about that evidence.
whyWrong.C: Whether the document was correct when uploaded is beside the point. The Project answers current questions, and a withdrawn tariff in knowledge will be used to answer them.
whyWrong.D: Restoring the document to the drive does not change the fact that it is withdrawn, and it creates a second copy of a superseded tariff — the situation the question is trying to resolve.

questions.mindset: When a superseded document is the only surviving copy, keep it but label it and say which document answers current questions.

questions.scenario: Kestrel Care's finance officer wants Claude to help reconcile a quarter's invoices. Her export contains every invoice the group received, including 60 belonging to one subsidiary that has since been sold and closed. The parent company's finance policy says closed-subsidiary material is retained for seven years but must not be shared outside the group.
questions.stem: Which assessment is MOST accurate?

options.text: The export is fine, because the reconciliation is internal and Claude is used under the group's own account.

The export should be reduced to the invoices needed for this quarter's reconciliation before it goes anywhere, with the closed subsidiary's material excluded unless the reconciliation genuinely requires it.
The whole export is acceptable because the invoices are already held in a company system and using Claude adds no new exposure.
Only the closed subsidiary's 60 invoices need removing, since the parent company's own invoices carry no sensitivity.

questions.explanation: The principle is **minimum necessary material for the task at hand**. Pasting an export of everything the group ever received into a shared assistant puts 60 invoices from a closed subsidiary into a system it was never intended to reach, for no benefit to a current reconciliation. Narrowing the data to what the job needs is standard practice and costs minutes. Note that it is the *relevance* that justifies the exclusion, not a claim that the parent's own invoices are somehow risk-free.

whyWrong.A: Internal use does not remove exposure: a copy now exists outside the group and outside the policy's boundary, and 'we own the account' is not a data-minimisation argument.
whyWrong.C: The material was already on company systems — the exposure created by pasting it is precisely the new copy. That reasoning would make every upload safe, which cannot be right.
whyWrong.D: It inverts the test. The question is what the reconciliation needs, not which department owns the data, and a wholesale export is broader than the job requires regardless of whose invoices are in it.

questions.mindset: Send only what the task needs — relevance to the job, not ownership of the data, decides what goes in.

questions.scenario: A nonprofit development officer has a shared drive containing 4,000 documents: grant guidelines, thank-you letters from a decade of funders, board minutes, staff files and photos from fundraising events. She wants one Project that can help her answer anything a colleague asks.
questions.stem: What is the BEST guidance for her?

options.text: Upload everything, since a broad knowledge base means fewer follow-up questions and more useful answers.
Upload nothing and paste what she needs per request, because a Project's knowledge should only ever hold a handful of documents.

Do not build one Project that covers everything. Scope it to the work — for example, funder guidelines and current templates — and keep staff records and personal photographs out of any Project's knowledge entirely.
Upload the guidelines and templates, then restrict the Project to colleagues so the staff files cannot be misused.

questions.explanation: A knowledge base should be **scoped to a job**, and personal material should not go into a Project's knowledge at all. Staff files and photos of identifiable people have no place in a fundraising assistant's sources, and no access setting makes that appropriate. Building several focused Projects — one for grant applications, one for donor communications — gives better answers for the work she actually does, because the relevant sources are unambiguous.

whyWrong.A: A broader base makes every answer more ambiguous, not less: the same question draws on board minutes, staff files and thank-you letters. It also puts sensitive material where it does not belong.
whyWrong.B: There is no rule that knowledge must be tiny, and the point of a Project is that the standing material lives in one place. Pasting per request reinstates the repetition a Project exists to remove.
whyWrong.D: Restriction controls who can ask questions; it does not change what is available to answer them. Personal files and identifiable photographs stay inappropriate as knowledge sources whoever is asking.

questions.mindset: Scope a knowledge base to a job, and keep personal records and identifiable images out of it whatever the access settings.

questions.scenario: An operations coordinator has Google Drive connected on her Claude Team workspace and asks Claude to find the answer to a question she is fairly sure is in the Q&A folder. She has never searched Drive successfully and does not know whether the document is a Doc, a Sheet or a PDF.
questions.stem: Which TWO statements about these preferences are accurate? Choose TWO.

options.text: The recommendation preference is being applied to colleagues' questions, so it is shaping answers about colleagues' projects — advice she is not in a position to give.
House style (spelling, units, punctuation) is true for the team's deliverables whatever any individual preference is, so it belongs with the Project rather than with her account.
Leave them all in place: account-wide preferences are personal, and a colleague who finds one unhelpful can simply ask a different question.
Move all four preferences into a Project for board business, so they apply only to board work.

questions.explanation: The four preferences are two different kinds of thing, and only one of them is causing trouble. The **recommendation rule is personal** — it is about how she wants to be answered — and because account-wide settings apply to everyone's chats in the workspace, it is being applied to colleagues' questions about colleagues' projects. **House style is organisational** — spelling, units and punctuation apply to the team's deliverables whoever is drafting — so it belongs with the work.

whyWrong.C: Treating it as purely personal misses that house style affects deliverables colleagues will see, and it leaves the recommendation rule applied to questions she has no standing to advise on.
whyWrong.D: Moving the preferences into a board Project narrows where they apply, which does not address the split, and it relocates a personal preference into what reads as team guidance.

questions.mindset: Split house style from personal preference: style belongs with the work, preferences belong with the individual.

questions.scenario: Redhaven Renewables' project office keeps one set of account-wide preferences across all of a manager's chats: answer in British English, use metric units, never use exclamation marks, and 'always give me a recommendation, not just options'. Her colleagues find the last one unhelpful when they ask neutral questions about a colleague's project.
questions.stem: What is the BEST way for the team to handle this?

options.text: Leave it. Account-wide preferences are personal, and a colleague who finds one unhelpful should simply ask a different question.

Move the preferences about house style — spelling, units, punctuation — into the team Project's instructions, and move 'always give me a recommendation' into that person's own settings, where it expresses a personal preference rather than a team rule.
Remove the preferences from both places and ask the team to type the relevant house style at the top of each request.
Keep all four preferences in account-wide settings and add a fifth saying colleagues may override the recommendation rule when they do not want one.

questions.explanation: The four preferences are two different kinds of thing. Spelling, units and punctuation are **house style** — they belong where the team's work is done, so they travel with the Project. 'Always give me a recommendation' is a **personal preference about how she wants to be answered**, and when applied to other people's questions it produces advice she is not entitled to give. Splitting them by kind fixes both problems at once.

whyWrong.A: Treating it as purely personal misses that house style affects deliverables colleagues will see. A team that has to correct spelling in outputs did not have a personal-preference problem.
whyWrong.C: Removing working preferences and asking people to retype them each time reinstates the repetition and guarantees the inconsistency the preferences existed to prevent.
whyWrong.D: Adding an override rule to a personal setting does not change whose preference it is, and it cannot stop it applying to questions asked by other people in the same workspace.

questions.mindset: Separate house style from personal preference: style belongs with the team's work, preferences belong with the individual.

questions.scenario: A grants officer's Project instructions are one sentence long: 'Be helpful and professional.' She has noticed that drafts arrive in inconsistent formats — sometimes a narrative, sometimes a table — and that some come back far too casual for a foundation that funds rural transport.
questions.stem: Which TWO changes would MOST improve this? Choose TWO.

options.text: Add the things that are true every time: which funders the Project serves, the required application structure and section order, the house tone for foundation-facing prose, and the length limit.
Add three approved applications the foundation has already funded, so the standard is visible rather than described.
Add 'be thorough' and 'use British English', since vagueness in the instructions is the cause of the inconsistency.
Leave the instructions short, and instead ask each request to state the format, the audience and the tone it needs.

questions.explanation: 'Helpful and professional' is not a specification — it is a mood, and the inconsistency is what happens when the request carries no criteria. Two changes fix it: **state the criteria that hold every time** (which funders, what structure, what tone, what length), which makes the output judgeable, and **show approved examples**, which demonstrate the standard far more reliably than adjectives do. The two are strongest together, and the rejected options either restate the vagueness or move the specification into every request.

whyWrong.C: 'Be thorough' is exactly the kind of instruction that adds length without adding criteria, and British English is already covered by house style elsewhere. It is the vague instruction the question is about.
whyWrong.D: Asking per request works but means every user rebuilds the specification each time and the answers will differ again. For rules that hold every time, that is the wrong place for them.

questions.mindset: Replace mood words with criteria that hold every time, and show approved examples rather than describing them.

questions.scenario: Two rules in a Project's instructions conflict. Rule one: 'Always give the full detail so nothing is missed.' Rule two: 'Answers must fit on one screen.' Officers report that some answers are exhaustive and others are clipped, with no pattern they can identify.
questions.stem: What is the BEST way to resolve this?

options.text: Keep both rules but move rule two to the top of the instruction set, since instructions earlier in a set tend to be followed more reliably.
Rewrite the two rules as one rule that states what to do when the detail and the limit conflict — for example, give the decision-relevant points first, then the detail that is genuinely needed.
Delete rule one, since a length limit is more useful to the reader than completeness.
Leave both rules and ask officers to mention in each request which one they mean, so Claude can follow the right one.

questions.explanation: Two rules that cannot both be satisfied produce **inconsistent behaviour by design** — the model resolves the conflict differently on different requests, which is exactly the unpatterned inconsistency described. The cure is to state the resolution rather than the conflict: what to lead with, what follows, and what to drop. That converts a coin-flip into a rule.

whyWrong.A: Position may influence emphasis, but it does not resolve a contradiction. Both rules still apply to the same request and the outcome stays unpredictable.
whyWrong.C: Deleting one rule removes the conflict by fiat and loses something the team wanted. Deciding which rule survives is a content decision that should be made deliberately, and the better outcome is usually an ordered rule rather than a deleted one.
whyWrong.D: Passing a flag per request makes every user resolve the team's policy for every question, and the answers will vary with what people type.

questions.mindset: When two instructions conflict, write the resolution into the instruction — do not rely on the model choosing consistently.

questions.scenario: A council's benefits team Project instructions now run to 90 lines. They include the full eligibility criteria for four schemes, three outreach tone guides for different audiences, a list of colleagues' pet names, a rule about never promising an appeal outcome, and a note that the team's phone lines close at 4pm. Recent answers have started omitting the appeal-right line and using an unfamiliar phrase.
questions.stem: What does this indicate, and what is the right response?

options.text: The instruction set is too long for its most important rules to be followed reliably. Sort the lines into what must always apply, what applies by audience, and what can be deleted or moved into a Project for the specific audience.
Nothing is wrong with the length. Add 'always include the appeal-rights line' at the end as well, so it is reinforced where it currently sits near the start.
The right response is to split the instruction set into two Projects so that each is under 45 lines.
Remove the colleagues' pet names and the phone-line hours first, then reassess whether the remaining length is a problem.

questions.explanation: When a compliance-critical rule starts being dropped, the problem is **attention inside a set nobody prunes** — the appeal-right line has to compete with 89 other lines. The response is to sort by durability and applicability: the rules that must always apply and the audience-specific guidance, which belongs in that audience's own Project. A required rule should not be one of ninety equally weighted lines.

whyWrong.B: Reinforcing a rule that is already being ignored, by adding it twice, treats an attention problem as a missing instruction. The appeal-right line is present and is still being dropped.
whyWrong.C: Splitting arbitrarily into two Projects still leaves a compliance rule competing with audience-specific detail, and it produces two configurations to maintain for one team.
whyWrong.D: Deleting the pet names is worthwhile housekeeping, but it does not address why the appeal-right line is being dropped, and it leaves the audience-splitting problem untouched.

questions.mindset: A required rule being ignored in a long instruction set is an attention problem — sort by what always applies, and move the rest out.

questions.scenario: Marden & Vale's managing director has used Claude for two years. His account-wide settings include a preference for short executive summaries and an instruction to always recommend a course of action. He now chairs a board that includes two non-executive directors who ask him to reproduce analyses in full, with sources shown.
questions.stem: What is the BEST adjustment?

options.text: Change the account-wide settings to match the strictest audience, so every output is safe for the board.
Keep the personal preference for concise summaries, and add an instruction that outputs must show sources for any figure used, so the fuller version is available without losing the concise default.
Ask the two non-executive directors to request full versions explicitly each time they want one.
Move all his settings into a Project for board business, so the preference applies only to board work.

questions.explanation: The two requirements are **compatible** and the fix is to satisfy both rather than trade one off. Concision is his preference about how to present; showing sources is a rule about what a figure must be traceable to. Keeping the concise default and adding a sourcing rule produces a short answer whose figures can be checked, which is what the non-executives actually asked for — not a longer answer.

whyWrong.A: Designing to the strictest audience makes every summary longer whether or not the reader needs it, and it discards a preference that is working. The requirements are not in genuine conflict.
whyWrong.C: This pushes a rule about his output onto the people reading it, and it guarantees the two directors get something different from him on the same analysis.
whyWrong.D: Moving settings into a Project narrows where they apply, which is useful for audience-specific content but does nothing for a board that meets in several settings, and it leaves the personal preference misplaced as team guidance.

questions.mindset: When two requirements look incompatible, look for the rule that satisfies both rather than choosing one audience's preference over the other's.

questions.scenario: Arikon Freight's driver handbook changed in April. The customer-service Project holds the handbook as knowledge, and its instructions also say 'the handbook describes the current rules — use them for any question about delivery or compliance.' Since April, agents have reported that answers about weekend delivery sound like the old rule.
questions.stem: Which TWO actions would address the underlying problem? Choose TWO.

options.text: Replace the handbook in the Project's knowledge with the current version, and remove the instruction that tells Claude to rely on the handbook, since uploaded documents cannot be treated as authoritative.
Replace the handbook with the current version and verify it by asking the Project a question whose answer only the new version can give.
Add the current weekend delivery rule to the end of the instructions as well, so agents get the answer even if the document is not read.
Ask the team to report the specific questions that produced outdated answers, and use those as the test set after the fix.

questions.explanation: Two distinct jobs. First, the **document itself must be current** — no amount of instruction makes a superseded handbook authoritative. Second, you need to know whether the fix worked, and the questions that already produced wrong answers are the natural test set: they are real, known-failing cases and cost nothing to collect. Copying one rule into the instructions and deleting the source document both trade a maintainable setup for a fragile one.

whyWrong.A: Removing the handbook discards the team's primary source for compliance questions and the instruction was doing useful work — the documents *are* treated as the authority, which is why they have to be current.
whyWrong.C: Copying the weekend rule into the instructions fixes one symptom permanently and leaves every other April change still wrong in the handbook, which is the actual failure mode.

questions.mindset: Fixing a stale knowledge base means updating the source and proving the fix on the questions that already failed.

questions.scenario: Ashgrove Legal's clause-drafting Projects were each set up by one person. A knowledge-management volunteer is now reviewing all of them and finds four with instructions written as a stream of one-off requests from 2022, each written for a single matter and never revisited.
questions.stem: Which TWO steps would MOST bring these back under control? Choose TWO.

options.text: Rewrite each instruction set from scratch, using her own judgement about what a clause-drafting Project ought to contain.
Go through each set line by line and ask of every line: is this true every time, is it audience-specific, or is it a one-off that should be deleted? Rebuild the sets from what survives.
Archive the four Projects and rebuild them once, at the end of the quarter, when there is time to do it properly.
Ask the fee-earners who used each Project to say which of its instructions still matter, and act on that.

questions.explanation: One-off rules are recognisable once you have the test — **is this true every time, is it audience-specific, or is it a single matter?** Applying it line by line converts a stream of incident-driven rules into a specification and keeps whatever was quietly doing real work. Asking the users who depended on those rules is the other half: they know which were load-bearing, and a review from them is what stops a tidy-up from removing something the team actually relies on. Together they triage and verify.

whyWrong.A: Starting from a blank page discards the accumulated knowledge about what this firm's clauses actually need, and the volunteer cannot see which historical rules were deliberate.
whyWrong.C: The Projects are in use now. Archiving them withdraws working tools from fee-earners who depend on them and defers a problem a line-by-line pass can address in an afternoon.

questions.mindset: Triage an instruction set line by line, then have the people who relied on it confirm what survives.

questions.scenario: Calder & Sons' Project for drafting customer quotations is shared with 25 staff. Six of them have added rules over eighteen months, some correct for their own region, one recommending a rate strategy the company abandoned in 2024. A new quotation clerk asks which instruction applies to her region.
questions.stem: What is the BEST response?

options.text: Ask a colleague in her region to tell her, since regional variation is best handled person to person.
Delete the abandoned rate strategy from the instructions immediately, and tell all 25 users the instruction set has been reviewed.
Say that she should assume the general rules apply and use her own judgement where her region differs, since the Project cannot hold regional detail.
Rewrite the instruction set so regional rules state their region explicitly, remove anything the company no longer follows, and tell all 25 users which regions each rule covers.

questions.explanation: This is an **ownership and visibility problem**: rules exist, they apply to a subset, and nobody can tell from the instruction set which. Making the region explicit in each rule turns them into something anyone can apply; removing abandoned guidance stops the Project recommending a strategy the company has left. And telling all 25 users what changed is part of the fix — an edit nobody is told about does not reach the people relying on the rules.

whyWrong.A: Regional variation is real but it does not need to live in one colleague's head. If it is written down with its region attached, a new clerk can apply it without knowing who to ask.
whyWrong.B: Removing the abandoned guidance is correct and necessary, and it is only part of the work. Announcing the review without fixing the regional scoping leaves the clerk's actual question unanswered.
whyWrong.C: Telling her to use her own judgement discards rules that were deliberately written for her region and pushes the burden onto the least experienced user.

questions.mindset: When rules apply to some users, say who — scope them explicitly and tell the users when the set changes.

questions.scenario: Rookwood Energy's project office keeps about 20 Projects. Each has one owner. Two owners have left in the last year and nobody has taken over their Projects, which now contain knowledge that is quietly going out of date. There is no record of who owns what.
questions.stem: Which TWO changes would MOST improve the situation? Choose TWO.

options.text: Maintain a short register — one line per Project: purpose, owner, the material it depends on and how fresh that material needs to be — and review it on a schedule.
Add a line to every Project's instructions saying 'check that your sources are current before answering', and rely on that.
Reassign the orphaned Projects to whoever most often asks questions in them.
Set a review rhythm: for each Project, an agreed interval at which its owner confirms the knowledge is current and retires anything superseded.

questions.explanation: The root problem is that Projects **age silently** — nothing about a Project announces that its knowledge is two years out of date. A register creates the visibility nobody has, because it names an owner per Project and states how fresh each dependency has to be. A review rhythm creates the mechanism, since 'refresh quarterly' and 'refresh when it changes' demand very different amounts of work. An instruction telling Claude to check currency cannot work: it has no way to know a source has changed.

whyWrong.B: The instruction cannot be carried out. Claude can tell the user a document says something; it has no way of knowing a policy document has been revised somewhere else, so the check is unmeetable by construction.
whyWrong.C: Frequency of use is a reasonable signal of who is closest to the work, and it is not ownership. Someone who asks the most questions may be a junior colleague, and an unowned Project would remain unowned.

questions.mindset: Configurations need a named owner and a refresh rhythm, because nothing about a Project signals that its material has aged.

questions.scenario: Ivybridge College's admissions team set up a Project to answer applicant questions in 2023, using the then-current course prospectus and an FAQ. The college has since renamed two courses, changed its entry requirements twice and closed one course entirely. The Project is still shared with current students.
questions.stem: What is the MOST appropriate first step?

options.text: Take the Project offline until the new prospectus is published, so nobody is given outdated information in the meantime.
Establish which of the three changes students are actually asking about now, and update or remove the affected material, prioritising by what is being asked.
Add an instruction to the Project saying 'the 2023 prospectus may be out of date; check with the admissions office before relying on it'.
Delete the Project, since a three-year-old configuration cannot be trusted and rebuilding once the new prospectus arrives would be cleaner.

questions.explanation: The Project serves real questions today, so the useful move is to work out **what is actually being asked and what is actually wrong**, then fix in that order. Recent student questions are evidence of where the configuration is failing, and they point at the material that matters. Taking it offline or deleting it withdraws a working tool from students precisely when they need it.

whyWrong.A: Withdrawing the Project removes the only route to help for exactly the students whose plans are affected, and the information is wrong in a small number of identifiable places, not everywhere.
whyWrong.C: An instruction asking users to check elsewhere makes the Project a signpost rather than an answer. Students are the group least likely to follow it, and it leaves the Project's own material wrong.
whyWrong.D: Deleting destroys working configuration and every correct part of it. Rebuilding once a new prospectus exists is a reasonable later option, but it is not the necessary first step and it is not obviously cleaner than updating.

questions.mindset: Prioritise stale configuration by what users are actually asking about, rather than withdrawing or rebuilding wholesale.

questions.scenario: A procurement specialist at Fenmoor Group built a Project to help colleagues check supplier invoices against purchase orders. She is leaving in a fortnight. The Project contains her own preferences as well as the company's rules, and no colleague knows how it is put together.
questions.stem: What should she do FIRST?

options.text: Hand it to a named colleague with a short handover note describing what each part of the configuration is for, and remove her personal preferences so only company rules remain.
Move the whole configuration into her own account so it survives her leaving the company.
Delete the Project, since without her it may not be used correctly and colleagues will ask her how it worked anyway.
Ask a colleague to reconstruct the Project from the output it has produced so far.

questions.explanation: The immediate risk is **configuration becoming unmanaged knowledge** the moment its author leaves. Naming an owner and writing down what each part is for converts an undocumented personal setup into something the company maintains. Removing her personal preferences matters as well: they were written for her, and colleagues inheriting them inherit preferences they did not choose and may not share.

whyWrong.B: The configuration dies with her employment in the normal way, and moving it into her personal account takes company purchasing rules and material out of the company's control — the opposite of a handover.
whyWrong.C: Deleting withdraws a working tool from colleagues two weeks before its author leaves, and it discards the accumulated rule set that colleagues are already relying on.
whyWrong.D: Reconstructing from outputs guesses at the rules that produced them. Outputs show results, not the criteria, and the reconstruction would be less accurate than a short note from the person who wrote them.

questions.mindset: Before you leave, name an owner and write down what each part of the configuration does — and leave only company rules in it.
